source_text: Regula exigit ueritatis ut primo omnium credamus in deum patrem et dominum omnipotentem, id est, rerum omnium perfectissimum conditorem, qui caelum alta sublimitate suspenderit, terram deiecta mole solidauerit, maria soluto liquore diffuderit, et haec omnia propriis et condignis instrumentis et ornata et plena digesserit. nam et in solidamento caeli luciferos solis ortus excitauit, lunae candentem globum ad solacium noctis mensurnis incrementis orbis impleuit, astrorum etiam radios uariis fulgoribus micantis lucis accendit: et haec omnia legitimis meatibus circumire totum mundi ambitum uoluit, humano generi dies, menses, annos, signa, tempora, utilitatesque factura. in terris quoque altissimos montes in uerticem sustulit, ualles in ima deiecit, campos aequaliter strauit, animalium greges ad uarias hominum seruitutes utiliter instituit. siluarum quoque robora humanis usibus profutura solidauit, fruges in cibum elicuit, fontium ora reserauit, et lapsuris fluminibus infudit. post quae, ne non etiam ipsis quoque deliciis procurasset oculorum, uariis florum coloribus ad uoluptatem spectantium cuncta uestiuit. in ipso quoque mari, quamuis esset et magnitudine et utilitate mirabile, multimoda animalia, nunc mediocris, nunc uasticorporis fingit, ingenium artificis de institutionis uarietate testantia. quibus non contentus, ne forte fremitus et cursus aquarum, cum dispendio possessoris humani, alienum occuparet elementum, fines litoribus inclusit: quo cum fremens fluctus et ex alto sinu spumans unda uenisset, rursum in se rediret nec terminos concessos excederet, seruans iura praescripta: ut diuinas leges tanto magis homo custodiret, quanto illas etiam elementa seruassent. Post quae hominem quoque mundo praeposuit et quidem ad imaginem dei factum: cui mentem et rationem indidit et prudentiam, ut deum posset imitari: cuius etsi corporis terrena primordia, caelestis tamen et diuini halitus inspirata substantia: quem, cum omnia in seruitutem illi dedisset, solum liberum esse uoluit. et ne in periculum caderet rursum soluta libertas, mandatum posuit, quo tamen non inesse malum fructu arboris doceretur, sed futurum, si forte, ex uoluntate hominis de contemptu datae legis praemonenam et liber esse debuerat, ne incongruenter dei imago seruiret: et lex addenda, ne usque ad contemptum dantis libertas effrenata prorumperet: ut et praemia condigna et merita poenarum consequenter exciperet, suum iam habens illud, quod motu mentis in alterutram partem agitare uoluisset. ex quo mortalitas, inuidia utique, in ipsum redit; qui cum illam de oboedientia posset euadere, in eandem incurrit, dum ex consilio peruerso deus esse festinat. cuius tamen poenam nihilominus indulgenter temperauit, dum non tam ipse, quam labores eius maledicuntur super terra. nam et quod requiritur, non ex ignorantia uenit, sed spem hominis futurae in Christo et inuentionis et salutis ostendit: et quod ne de ligno arboris uitae contingat arcetur, non de inuidiae maligno liuore descendit, sed ne uiuens in aeternum, nisi peccata Christus ante donasset, circumferret secum in poenam sui semper immortale delictum. Quamquam etiam superioribus, id est, super ipsum quoque solidamentum partibus, quae non sunt hodie nostris contemplabiles oculis, angelos prius instituerit, spiritales uirtutes digesserit, thronos potestatesque praefecerit, et alia multa caelorum immensa spatia et sacramentorum infinita opera condiderit, ut immensus hic licet mundus paene nouissimum magis dei corporalium rerum appareat opus esse, quam solum, namque quae infra terram iacent, neque ipsa sunt digestis et ordinatis potestatibus uacua. locus enim est quo piorum animae impiorumque ducuntur, futuri iudicii praeiudicia sentientes: ut operum ipsius in omnibus partibus redundantes magnitudines non intra mundi huius capacissimos licet, ut diximus, sinus conclusas uideremus, sed etiam infra ipsius mundi et profunda et altitudines cogitare possemus; et sic considerata operum magnitudine, tantae molis digne mirari possemus artificem.
pass_a_gloss: The rule of truth demands that first of all we believe in God the Father and Lord, all-powerful, that is, the most perfect creator of all things, who has suspended the heaven with lofty sublimity, solidified the earth with its cast-down mass, poured out the seas with their fluid liquid, and has arranged and filled all these things with their own and suitable instruments. For also in the solidification of the heaven, He has excited the light-bringing risings of the sun, filled the shining globe of the moon with measured increments of the orbit for the solace of night, and ignited the rays of the stars with varied brilliances of sparkling light. And He has willed that all these things go around the whole circuit of the world in legitimate courses, making days, months, years, signs, times, and utilities for the human race. On the earth also, He has lifted up the highest mountains to the top, cast down the valleys to the bottom, spread out the fields equally, and usefully instituted the herds of animals for various human services. He has also solidified the strength of the forests for human uses, brought forth the crops for food, opened the mouths of the fountains, and poured into the flowing rivers. After these things, lest He not also have provided for the delights of the eyes themselves, He has clothed all things with varied colors of flowers for the pleasure of the spectators. In the sea also, although it was wonderful in magnitude and utility, He has fashioned many kinds of animals, now of moderate size, now of vast body, testifying to the ingenuity of the artisan from the variety of institutions. Not content with these things, lest perhaps the roar and course of the waters, with the loss of the human possessor, might occupy an alien element, He has enclosed the shores with boundaries, so that when the foaming wave and the frothy surge came, it would return into itself and not exceed the granted limits, keeping the prescribed laws, so that man might keep the divine laws all the more, since even the elements kept them. After these things, He also set man over the world, and indeed made him in the image of God, to whom He gave a mind and reason and prudence, so that he might imitate God. Although the earthly beginnings of his body are of the earth, yet the substance of his breath is inspired by the heavenly and divine, and He willed that he, to whom He had given all things in servitude, should be the only free one. And lest he fall into danger, with his freedom once more loosened, He put a command, by which, however, the evil of the fruit of the tree was not taught to be present, but future, if perhaps, from the will of man, from contempt of the given law, a warning was given, and he ought to be free, lest the image of God serve incongruously. And the law was added, lest the unbridled freedom burst forth even to contempt of the giver, so that he might receive the suitable rewards and the deserved punishments, having that which he had willed to stir up by the motion of his mind in either direction. From this, mortality, certainly, returns to him, who, since he could have escaped from obedience, rushes into the same, while hastening to be God from perverted counsel. Nevertheless, God has tempered his punishment indulgently, since not he himself, but his labors are cursed above the earth. For what is required does not come from ignorance, but shows the hope of man for the future in Christ and the invention and salvation, and what is forbidden, lest it touch the wood of the tree of life, does not come from the malignant envy, but lest, living eternally, he might carry with him in punishment his always immortal sin, unless Christ had previously given sins. Although even in the things above, that is, above the solidification itself, in the parts which are not visible to our eyes today, He had previously instituted angels, arranged spiritual powers, appointed thrones and powers, and founded many other immense spaces of the heavens and infinite works of sacraments, so that this immense world, although it may seem to be the latest, rather appears to be the bodily work of God, not alone, for the things that lie beneath the earth are not empty of arranged and ordered powers. For there is a place where the souls of the pious and the impious are led, experiencing the pre-judgments of the future judgment, so that we might not see the overflowing magnitudes of His works only within the most capacious bosom of this world, but also consider them beneath the world and in its depths and heights, and thus, considering the magnitude of the works, we might be able to wonder worthily at the artisan of such great works.
pass_b_english: The rule of truth demands that we first of all believe in God the Father and Lord, the Almighty, that is, the most perfect Creator of all things. He suspended the heavens with lofty height, solidified the earth with its downward mass, poured out the seas with their liquid fluid, and arranged and filled all these things with their own proper and suitable instruments. Indeed, in the solidification of the heavens, He kindled the light-bringing risings of the sun, filled the shining globe of the moon with measured increments of its orbit for the solace of night, and ignited the rays of the stars with varied brilliances of sparkling light. He also willed that all these things traverse the whole circuit of the world in legitimate courses, making days, months, years, signs, seasons, and utilities for the human race.

On the earth also, He lifted up the highest mountains to the summit, cast down the valleys to the bottom, spread out the plains equally, and usefully instituted herds of animals for various human services. He also solidified the strength of the forests for human uses, brought forth crops for food, opened the mouths of the fountains, and poured water into the flowing rivers. After these things, lest He not also have provided for the delights of the eyes themselves, He clothed all things with the varied colors of flowers for the pleasure of the spectators.

In the sea also, although it was wonderful in both magnitude and utility, He fashioned many kinds of animals, now of moderate size, now of vast body, testifying to the ingenuity of the Artisan from the variety of their creation. Not content with these things, lest perhaps the roar and course of the waters, with the loss of the human possessor, might occupy an alien element, He enclosed the shores with boundaries. He did this so that when the foaming wave and the frothy surge came from the deep, they would return into themselves and not exceed the granted limits, keeping the prescribed laws, so that man might keep the divine laws all the more, since even the elements kept them.

After these things, He also set man over the world, and indeed made him in the image of God. To him He gave a mind, reason, and prudence, so that he might imitate God. Although the earthly beginnings of his body are of the earth, yet the substance of his breath is inspired by the heavenly and divine. He willed that the one to whom He had given all things in servitude should be the only free one. And lest he fall into danger with his freedom once more loosened, He put a command in place. By this command, however, the evil of the fruit of the tree was not taught to be present, but future, if perhaps from the will of man, from contempt of the given law. A warning was given, and he ought to be free, lest the image of God serve incongruously. And the law was added, lest unbridled freedom burst forth even to contempt of the Giver, so that he might receive the suitable rewards and the deserved punishments, having that which he had willed to stir up by the motion of his mind in either direction.

From this, mortality certainly returns to him. Although he could have escaped it through obedience, he rushes into it, while hastening to be God from perverted counsel. Nevertheless, God has tempered his punishment indulgently, since not he himself, but his labors, are cursed above the earth. For what is required does not come from ignorance, but shows the hope of man for the future in Christ, both of discovery and of salvation. And what is forbidden, lest he touch the wood of the tree of life, does not come from malignant envy, but lest, living eternally, he might carry with him in punishment his always immortal sin, unless Christ had previously given remission of sins.

Although even in the things above, that is, above the solidification itself, in the parts which are not visible to our eyes today, He had previously instituted angels, arranged spiritual powers, appointed thrones and powers, and founded many other immense spaces of the heavens and infinite works of sacraments, so that this immense world, although it may seem to be the latest, rather appears to be the bodily work of God, not alone. For the things that lie beneath the earth are not empty of arranged and ordered powers. For there is a place where the souls of the pious and the impious are led, experiencing the pre-judgments of the future judgment. This is so that we might not see the overflowing magnitudes of His works only within the most capacious bosom of this world, but also consider them beneath the world and in its depths and heights. And thus, considering the magnitude of the works, we might be able to wonder worthily at the Artisan of such great works.
